# Turn whatever's left in your fridge into a real recipe with Le Chat

> **In short:** Le Chat is Mistral's AI assistant — type in what's left in your fridge and it will suggest a real recipe you can cook tonight. There's a free option to start, no install required, and most people get a usable answer in under a minute. It can't taste your food, but it can spark a meal you'd actually want to eat. Note: Mistral now calls this assistant **Vibe** (formerly Le Chat) — you may see either name in the app and on mistral.ai.

You've stared into the fridge at 6 p.m., seen three random vegetables, half a bag of pasta, and some questionable cheese. No plan. No energy for a grocery run. This guide shows you how to hand that mess to Le Chat and walk away with a real recipe in about five minutes — even if you've never opened an AI assistant before.

## Before you start
- **A free Le Chat account.** You can sign up with an email address or a Google/Apple account at Mistral's site. The basic plan is enough for recipe questions; paid plans exist for heavier use, but you don't need one tonight.
- **A phone, tablet, or computer with internet.** Le Chat works in any web browser, and there's also a mobile app if you'd rather cook from your phone.
- **Roughly 5 minutes.** Most of that is the chat itself thinking.
- **No cooking skills required** — but it helps if you know roughly what equipment you have (a stove, an oven, a microwave, nothing fancier).

## Step 1 — Open Le Chat and start a fresh chat
Open your browser and go to Le Chat (Mistral's chat assistant). If you're on a phone, you can also use the Le Chat app. Once you arrive, you'll see a clean screen with a text box near the bottom — that's where you type your message. Look for a button or link that says something like **"New chat"** or **"Start a new conversation"** if you see leftover messages from earlier; a fresh chat keeps your recipe ideas separate from anything else you've asked about.

If you're not logged in yet, you'll be asked to sign up or log in first. An email address is enough — no credit card needed for the basic option. **If it looks different on your device:** the layout is similar on mobile and desktop, but on smaller screens the text box usually sits at the bottom of the screen, and menus may be tucked behind a **☰ icon** in the corner.

💬 Example: you don't need to type anything yet — just confirm a fresh, empty chat is ready.

**You'll know it worked when** you see an empty chat screen with a clear text box and no old messages above it.

## Step 2 — Tell Le Chat what's actually in your fridge
Tap inside the text box and type a list of ingredients you have on hand. Don't worry about being neat — Le Chat understands plain lists, short sentences, even messy notes like "a bit of sour cream, maybe 2 days left." Mention the main items, how much of each you roughly have, and anything you definitely do **not** want to use (stale bread, sad lettuce). Then send the message by tapping the **send** arrow or pressing **Enter** on a keyboard.

A short pause — usually a few seconds — and a reply appears underneath your message. The assistant reads what you wrote and starts to think about combinations. **If it looks different on your device:** the send button might be a paper-airplane icon, a circle with an arrow, or just the **Enter** key on a physical keyboard.

💬 Example: copy and adapt this — *"Here's what's in my fridge: 2 eggs, half an onion, a handful of spinach, leftover cooked rice (about 1 cup), some grated cheddar, soy sauce, and one tortilla. I don't want anything too spicy. What can I make for dinner for 1 person?"*

**You'll know it worked when** you see a written reply that names at least one specific dish based on your ingredients.

## Step 3 — Ask for the details you actually need to cook it
The first reply usually gives a quick idea, but you still need a real recipe — amounts, steps, time. Ask a follow-up question in the same chat. Mention how many people you're cooking for, how much time you have, and any tools you want to use (one pan, an oven, no oven, etc.). The more useful detail you give here, the more useful the recipe will be.

Because you're still in the same conversation, Le Chat already knows your ingredients — you don't have to repeat them. Just tell it what shape you want the answer in. **If it looks different on your device:** if the chat stops mid-answer, look for a small **"continue"** or **"regenerate"** button at the end of the message.

💬 Example: *"Great idea — please give me a full step-by-step recipe for the rice omelette. I'm cooking for 1, I have about 25 minutes, only a frying pan and a spatula, and I'd like it written as numbered steps."*

**You'll know it worked when** the reply includes a recipe title, ingredient amounts, numbered cooking steps, and a rough total time.

## Step 4 — Tweak the recipe if something doesn't fit
Read the recipe. If an ingredient is missing, a step feels too hard, or a measurement looks off, just ask. This is the moment where AI cooking help really pays off — you can ask for a swap, a simpler method, a vegetarian version, or a faster version, all without starting over. The assistant keeps the whole conversation in mind, so it will adjust what it already wrote.

Think of it like texting a friend who actually answers back: short, clear messages work best. Tell it the **one thing** you want to change, and let it respond. **If it looks different on your device:** if a reply is too long to fit on screen, scroll up and down within the message; some apps also have a **copy** button near the answer.

💬 Example: *"I don't have soy sauce — can you swap in Worcestershire sauce instead? And can you make it ready in 15 minutes instead of 25?"*

**You'll know it worked when** the new version of the recipe reflects your changes (different sauce, shorter timing) and still makes sense as a meal.

## Step 5 — Save the recipe so you can actually cook it
When you're happy with the answer, keep it somewhere you can read while you cook. You can copy the recipe to your notes app, take a screenshot, or just leave the chat open on a counter-friendly device. If you start a new chat later, your old conversation won't be the focus — so saving it yourself is the safest move.

If you want, you can also ask for a shopping list for the next time you cook it, or ask how to store leftovers. **If it looks different on your device:** on phones, a long press on the answer often brings up a copy option; on computers, right-click works the same way.

💬 Example: *"Can you give me a short grocery list for next time I make this, and tell me how to store leftovers in the fridge?"*

**You'll know it worked when** the recipe is sitting somewhere you can reach while standing at the stove — on your phone, a printout, or a notes app.

## Common mistakes
- **Listing ingredients without saying how much.** "Some chicken" gives a vague answer. Even rough amounts — *"about 150 g of chicken"* — make the recipe much more useful.
- **Forgetting to mention dietary needs or allergies.** If you can't eat nuts, dairy, or gluten, say so in your first message. It's easier than asking for a swap later.
- **Starting a brand-new chat for every follow-up.** Stay in the same conversation so the assistant remembers your ingredients. A new chat makes it forget everything and you'll have to repeat yourself.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** this turns "I have nothing to eat" into a real dinner in the time it takes to boil water. It also helps you use up food before it goes bad, which saves money and reduces waste.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is to open Le Chat right now and paste the example prompt from Step 2, swapping in whatever is actually in your fridge tonight. You don't need to plan ahead — the messier your real-life fridge, the better the test.

## Try it now
Open Le Chat, list three to five ingredients you have at home right now, and ask for a dinner recipe for one person. Cook the result tonight — no grocery run required.
